title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Rents are falling now, so the housing crisis is over.

Rebuttal: True, national rents dipped about 0.5% in early 2026. But asking rents for professionally managed apartments were still 29% above 2020, and a record 22.7 million renter households were cost-burdened in 2024. A small dip at the top of a mountain isn't the valley.

Sources: Harvard JCHS, State of the Nation's Housing 2026, NLIHC, Memo to Members on JCHS 2026

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: People should just work more if they can't afford rent.

Rebuttal: Work matters, and most renters do work. But NLIHC's 2026 housing wage for a two-bedroom is $34.73 an hour, and the average renter earns $24.84. In Louisiana, a minimum-wage worker would need about 121 hours a week. There aren't enough hours.

Sources: NLIHC, Out of Reach 2026, NLIHC, Out of Reach 2026: Louisiana

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Young people can't buy homes because they spend too much on avocado toast and phones.

Rebuttal: Spending choices matter at the margins. But the typical home cost about 3.2 years of income in the 1990s and 5.0 years in 2024. From 2019 to 2024 prices rose 48% while incomes rose 22%. The median first-time buyer is now 40.

Sources: Harvard JCHS, Home Prices Surge to Five Times Median Income, 2025, NAR, 2025 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Wall Street giants are buying up all the houses.

Rebuttal: Fair concern, but be accurate. Investors bought about 29% to 32% of homes in early 2025, yet large investors were only about 3% of purchases; small ones dominate. The fix isn't only aimed at big firms. It's putting families first: owner-occupant priority, limits on bulk buys and public housing.

Sources: Cotality, Investor Purchase Indicator, 2025, Harvard JCHS, State of the Nation's Housing 2026

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: RealPage was found guilty of rent price-fixing.

Rebuttal: Not accurate. DOJ alleged RealPage's software helped landlords coordinate rents. RealPage denied it and settled in November 2025 without admitting wrongdoing or paying a penalty, agreeing to limits on nonpublic data and oversight. No court found guilt. The allegations still matter, which is why states like New York banned this software.

Sources: The Real Deal, RealPage Settles Antitrust Lawsuit with DOJ, 2025, Law360, judge approves DOJ-RealPage deal, 2026

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Rent algorithms just help landlords price efficiently, like any business.

Rebuttal: Pricing software can be legal. The problem DOJ alleged was competitors feeding private data into one shared tool that recommends rents. Greystar agreed to stop using rivals' nonpublic data and paid $7 million to nine states. New York banned such tools in 2025. Efficiency for landlords can mean higher rent for everyone.

Sources: California Attorney General, Greystar $7 million settlement, 2025, New York algorithmic rent-setting ban coverage, October 2025

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Rent control always destroys housing.

Rebuttal: It has real tradeoffs. A Stanford study of San Francisco found covered landlords cut rental supply by 15%, raising citywide rents about 5.1%. The same study found tenants were nearly 20% more likely to stay in their homes. So pair stabilization with new-construction exemptions, anti-conversion rules and public building.

Sources: Diamond, McQuade and Qian, NBER Working Paper 24181, 2019, Minnesota Reformer, St. Paul walks back rent control, 2025

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: St. Paul proves rent control is a disaster.

Rebuttal: St. Paul's strict 2021 cap was followed by a sharp construction drop, and the city exempted new buildings. That's a real lesson in design. But neighboring Minneapolis, without rent control, saw an even steeper construction drop in 2024, so high interest rates mattered too. Design stabilization carefully. Don't abandon tenants.

Sources: Minnesota Reformer, St. Paul walks back rent control, 2025, Pew Charitable Trusts, Minneapolis land use reforms, 2024

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Zoning has nothing to do with affordability. It's all greedy landlords.

Rebuttal: Landlord power is real. So is supply. Pew found Minneapolis grew housing 12% from 2017 to 2022 after zoning and parking reforms, and rents rose 1% versus 14% in the rest of Minnesota. We need both: more homes and tenant power.

Sources: Pew Charitable Trusts, 2024, Harvard JCHS, State of the Nation's Housing 2026

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: If we just let the market build, housing will become affordable for everyone.

Rebuttal: More building helps. But the market isn't building for the bottom. Apartments under $1,000 fell about 30% from 2014 to 2024 adjusting for inflation, and there are only 35 affordable homes per 100 extremely low-income renters. The lowest rungs need public and social housing.

Sources: Harvard JCHS, State of the Nation's Housing 2026, NLIHC, The Gap 2026

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Anyone who needs housing help can get Section 8.

Rebuttal: No. Only about one in four eligible households gets federal rental help. About 13.8 million eligible households got none in 2023. In one national survey, nearly half of voucher waiting lists were closed to new applicants.

Sources: Harvard JCHS, State of the Nation's Housing 2026, PAHRC, Housing Agency Waiting Lists and the Demand for Housing Assistance, 2016

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Government spends too much helping people with housing.

Rebuttal: It spends a lot, but mostly on the comfortable. The mortgage interest deduction cost about $52.6 billion in 2025, and households over $200,000 got 78% of it. Meanwhile three out of four eligible poor renters get nothing.

Sources: Congressional Research Service IF13190, 2026 (citing JCT), NLIHC, Out of Reach 2026

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: The mortgage interest deduction helps the middle class become homeowners.

Rebuttal: Some middle-class families do benefit. But 96.8% of the benefit goes to households over $100,000, and 78.2% to those over $200,000. It mainly rewards buying bigger houses for people who already can. A credit for first-time buyers would do more for the middle.

Sources: Congressional Research Service IF13190, 2026 (citing JCT), Tax Policy Center, Benefits of the Mortgage Interest and Property Tax Deductions

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Public housing failed and should be torn down.

Rebuttal: Some projects were badly run. But Congress capped public housing at 1999 levels and underfunded repairs until the backlog hit an estimated $50 billion or more. Stock fell to about 884,000 units. You can't starve a program and then call it a failure.

Sources: NLIHC, Advocates' Guide 2025: Public Housing, Quality Housing and Work Responsibility Act of 1998

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Social housing only works in small, rich European cities.

Rebuttal: Vienna is wealthy, and it's a city, not a nation. But Singapore housed 77.2% of resident households in public flats in 2025 with 91.2% homeownership. Big public housing systems can work when they're funded and designed well.

Sources: Singapore Department of Statistics, 2025, City of Vienna, socialhousing.wien

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Evictions only happen to people who don't pay rent.

Rebuttal: Most evictions are for nonpayment, yes. That's the point: rents outran wages. Eviction Lab tracked 1.23 million filings in 2025 in sites covering a third of renters. And many tenants have defenses they never raise because about 4% have a lawyer versus 83% of landlords.

Sources: Eviction Lab, Eviction Tracking System 2025 report, NLIHC, Advocates' Guide 2026: Right to Counsel

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Right to counsel is too expensive for cities.

Rebuttal: It costs money up front. But evictions cost cities too, through shelters, emergency rooms and lost school days. New York City's filings fell from about 247,000 in 2013 to about 118,000 in 2024, and most represented tenants stayed housed.

Sources: New York City Comptroller, Evictions Up, Representation Down, 2025, National Coalition for a Civil Right to Counsel, NYC right to counsel

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Louisiana's eviction laws are fair to both sides.

Rebuttal: Landlords do need a way to recover unpaid rent. But Louisiana allows just five days' notice to vacate for nonpayment, leases can waive that notice, and tenants can have about 24 hours to leave after judgment. That's speed built for one side.

Sources: Louisiana Law Help, Evictions, Eviction Lab, ETS 2025 report

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Homelessness is mostly about addiction and mental illness.

Rebuttal: Addiction and mental illness are real and need treatment. But HUD counted 230,366 people in families with children in 2025. Places with similar addiction rates have very different homelessness rates. Housing costs drive the numbers.

Sources: HUD, 2025 Annual Homelessness Assessment Report, NLIHC, The Gap 2026

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Homelessness programs never work.

Rebuttal: Not true. HUD's 2025 count found family homelessness fell 11% from 2024 and veteran homelessness hit a record low. When we fund housing, it works. Cutting it is a choice.

Sources: HUD, 2025 Annual Homelessness Assessment Report, NLIHC, Memo to Members on 2025 AHAR

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Short-term rentals help New Orleans homeowners make ends meet.

Rebuttal: Some owners do rely on that income. That's why the city allows one per block with an operator living on site. But whole homes turned into hotels pull housing out of neighborhoods. The federal appeals court largely upheld the city's rules in 2025.

Sources: U.S. Fifth Circuit ruling, October 7, 2025, via Biz New Orleans, Kean Miller, Louisiana Law Blog, 2025

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: High insurance in Louisiana is just about hurricanes. Nothing can be done.

Rebuttal: Storms drive real risk. But policy shapes the price: a dozen insurers failed after 2020–21, and rates rose 16.2% in 2022 and 14% in 2023. A Newrez analysis put Louisiana's average premium at about $4,238 in 2025, the nation's highest. Fortified roofs, public reinsurance and rate oversight are choices.

Sources: Louisiana Department of Insurance statement via KPLC, 2026, Newrez analysis via Scotsman Guide, 2026

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Renters don't pay property insurance, so it's not their problem.

Rebuttal: Renters don't buy the landlord's policy, true. But landlords pass costs into rent. Average monthly home insurance premiums nationally rose 72% from 2019 to 2025. Every insurance hike shows up in the lease renewal.

Sources: Harvard JCHS, State of the Nation's Housing 2026, Newrez analysis via Scotsman Guide, 2026

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: The racial homeownership gap is about personal choices, not discrimination.

Rebuttal: Choices vary for every family. But the gap is large and persistent: 74.5% white non-Hispanic versus 45.4% Black homeownership in mid-2026. Federal redlining and unequal lending shaped that wealth for generations.

Sources: U.S. Census Bureau, HVS Q2 2026, Harvard JCHS, State of the Nation's Housing 2026

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Tenant unions just cause trouble and drive up rents.

Rebuttal: Conflict with landlords can be uncomfortable. But tenant organizing has won right to counsel laws in 26 jurisdictions and helped pass bans on rent-setting algorithms. Collective bargaining gets repairs and fair treatment that one tenant alone can't.

Sources: NLIHC, Advocates' Guide 2026: Right to Counsel, New York algorithmic rent-setting ban coverage, October 2025

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Housing isn't a right. Nothing is free.

Rebuttal: Housing costs money to build, true. So do roads, schools and fire departments, and we call those public goods. Vienna and Singapore house large shares of their people through public systems. A right means a guarantee, not a free lunch.

Sources: City of Vienna, socialhousing.wien, Singapore Department of Statistics, 2025

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Immigrants are causing the housing shortage.

Rebuttal: Population growth does raise demand. But immigration fell about 50% in 2025, and rents remained 29% above 2020. Shortages come from decades of underbuilding, zoning limits and lost public housing. Blaming neighbors builds zero homes.

Sources: Harvard JCHS, State of the Nation's Housing 2026, NLIHC, Memo to Members on JCHS 2026

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Homeowners are doing fine. Only renters struggle.

Rebuttal: Homeowners have more wealth on average. But 20.7 million homeowner households were cost-burdened in 2024, up 4 million since 2019, driven by taxes and insurance. This is a shared squeeze.

Sources: Harvard JCHS, State of the Nation's Housing 2026, Smart Cities Dive summary of JCHS 2026

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: First-time buyers are fine; they just wait a bit longer now.

Rebuttal: Waiting isn't fatal. But first-time buyers fell to a record-low 21% of purchases, and their median age hit 40. Under-35 homeownership fell to 35.2% in mid-2026. Every lost year is lost equity.

Sources: NAR, 2025 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers, U.S. Census Bureau, HVS Q2 2026

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Build-to-rent gives families more choices.

Rebuttal: Some families want to rent a house, and that's fine. But build-to-rent reached 11% of new single-family homes in 2025, nearly three times its historical average. When more new houses are never for sale, ownership shrinks.

Sources: Harvard JCHS, State of the Nation's Housing 2026, Cotality, Investor Purchase Indicator, 2025

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Corporate landlords provide better service than mom-and-pop landlords.

Rebuttal: Some do have better maintenance systems. But Invitation Homes paid $48 million in 2024 to settle FTC charges over hidden fees and unfair practices, without admitting wrongdoing. Size brings power, and power needs accountability.

Sources: Federal Trade Commission, Invitation Homes settlement, 2024, Harvard JCHS, State of the Nation's Housing 2026

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Louisiana renters have it easy because the cost of living is low.

Rebuttal: Rents are lower here than in big coastal cities. But wages are lower too. NLIHC finds the Louisiana renter's mean wage is about $18.27, against a $21.88 housing wage. And 48.4% of Louisiana renters were cost-burdened in 2023.

Sources: NLIHC, Out of Reach 2026: Louisiana, LSU Shreveport CBER, 2025

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: The minimum wage doesn't matter for housing.

Rebuttal: Most renters earn more than $7.25. But at that floor, a Louisiana worker would need about 121 hours a week for a two-bedroom. And 17 of the 25 most common jobs pay less than the one-bedroom housing wage nationally. Wages and rents are one fight.

Sources: NLIHC, Out of Reach 2026, NLIHC, Out of Reach 2026: Louisiana

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Public housing in New Orleans was demolished because it was beyond repair.

Rebuttal: Some buildings had real damage from Katrina. But many sturdy brick buildings were demolished anyway after a December 2007 council vote, and redevelopments brought fewer deeply affordable units. Residents who wanted to come home were shut out.

Sources: HUD, New Orleans public housing redevelopment records, NLIHC, Advocates' Guide 2025: Public Housing

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: The Census delay doesn't matter to regular people.

Rebuttal: Most people never open a Census table. But the American Community Survey measures rent burden in every parish and guides federal funding. In August 2026 the Bureau said the 2025 release date was still being determined, and more than 100 organizations objected.

Sources: U.S. Census Bureau media advisory, August 4, 2026, The Census Project letter, September 4, 2026

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Climate risk is overblown in housing.

Rebuttal: Projections vary. But Harvard's Joint Center, using FEMA's risk index, found 72 million homes face at least moderate risk of climate disaster losses, and insurance premiums rose 72% from 2019 to 2025. In Louisiana we pay that bill already.

Sources: Harvard JCHS, State of the Nation's Housing 2026, FEMA, National Risk Index

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Vouchers are enough. We don't need to build public housing.

Rebuttal: Vouchers work well for families who get them. But only about one in four eligible households do, and a voucher can't create an apartment that doesn't exist. With 35 affordable homes per 100 extremely low-income renters, we need both.

Sources: NLIHC, The Gap 2026, Harvard JCHS, State of the Nation's Housing 2026

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Renters are just people who haven't worked hard enough to own.

Rebuttal: Some people choose to rent, and that's fine. But home prices rose to 5 times income in 2024, and the median first-time buyer is 40. Nurses, teachers and welders rent because the ladder got pulled up.

Sources: Harvard JCHS, Home Prices Surge to Five Times Median Income, 2025, NAR, 2025 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Tenants have plenty of rights already.

Rebuttal: Some tenants do, in some places. But only 26 jurisdictions guarantee a lawyer in eviction court. Nationally about 4% of tenants have one versus 83% of landlords. In Louisiana, a lease can waive even the five-day notice to vacate.

Sources: NLIHC, Advocates' Guide 2026: Right to Counsel, Louisiana Law Help, Evictions

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Banning rent algorithms is government overreach.

Rebuttal: Regulation should be careful. But antitrust law has always barred competitors from coordinating prices. New York's 2025 ban targets software using rivals' nonpublic data, the same practice Greystar agreed to stop. That's defending competition, not ending it.

Sources: New York algorithmic rent-setting ban coverage, October 2025, California Attorney General, Greystar settlement, 2025

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Raising wages will just lead landlords to raise rents.

Rebuttal: Landlords charge what the market bears, true. That's why wages alone aren't enough. But when the average renter earns $24.84 and the housing wage is $34.73, the gap is too big to close any other way. Raise pay, build homes, protect tenants.

Sources: NLIHC, Out of Reach 2026, NLIHC, The Gap 2026

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Homelessness is a big-city problem, not a Louisiana one.

Rebuttal: Big cities do have the largest counts. But Louisiana has the nation's highest poverty rate and an 8% eviction filing rate in New Orleans. One storm or one eviction can push a family out anywhere.

Sources: Eviction Lab, ETS 2025 report, HUD, 2025 Annual Homelessness Assessment Report

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Insurance companies left Louisiana because of lawyers and fraud.

Rebuttal: Litigation costs were a real factor, and Louisiana passed reforms. But a dozen insurers failed after the 2020–21 storms because of catastrophic losses and thin capital. Rate hikes slowed to 4.4% in 2025, yet the average premium still led the nation. Homeowners need a public backstop, not just tort reform.

Sources: Louisiana Department of Insurance statement via KPLC, 2026, Newrez analysis via Scotsman Guide, 2026

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Investors improve neighborhoods by fixing up homes.

Rebuttal: Some investors do renovate and rent at fair prices. But when investors buy nearly a third of homes, first-time buyers face cash competition, and first-time buyers fell to a record-low 21% of purchases. Priority for owner-occupants protects both.

Sources: Cotality, Investor Purchase Indicator, 2025, NAR, 2025 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Affordable housing lowers nearby property values.

Rebuttal: Neighbors worry about that sincerely. But Minneapolis allowed more homes, grew housing 12%, and kept rents nearly flat. Good design and stable residents help neighborhoods. Fear shouldn't zone out nurses and cooks.

Sources: Pew Charitable Trusts, 2024, Harvard JCHS, State of the Nation's Housing 2026

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Waiting lists are long because people abuse the system.

Rebuttal: Every program needs oversight. But lists are long because funding covers about a quarter of eligible households. In one national survey 2.8 million families waited for vouchers and 48.4% of voucher lists were closed.

Sources: PAHRC via NLIHC, 2016, Harvard JCHS, State of the Nation's Housing 2026

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Rent stabilization means landlords can never raise rents.

Rebuttal: That's not how most modern laws work. Oregon's 2019 statewide law and California's 2019 law allow yearly increases tied to inflation with a cap, and exempt newer buildings. They limit spikes, not all increases.

Sources: Oregon Senate Bill 608, 2019, California Assembly Bill 1482, 2019

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Tenant organizing is illegal or dangerous.

Rebuttal: Some landlords retaliate, and tenants should know the risks. But meeting with neighbors, petitioning, and bargaining together are legal activities. Document everything, call legal aid, and act as a group. Organized tenants won right to counsel across 26 jurisdictions.

Sources: NLIHC, Advocates' Guide 2026: Right to Counsel, National Coalition for a Civil Right to Counsel

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Nothing will ever fix the housing crisis.

Rebuttal: It's a hard problem. But we have proof that change works: NYC eviction filings were cut roughly in half, Minneapolis held rents steady while building, family homelessness fell 11% in 2025, and Vienna has housed half its people for generations. Organized people made each one happen.

Sources: New York City Comptroller, 2025, HUD, 2025 Annual Homelessness Assessment Report

title: Claude Drop: housing-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Tenant protections just make landlords stop renting.

Rebuttal: Some small landlords do sell when rules tighten, and that's worth watching. But New York City's right to counsel cut eviction filings from about 247,000 in 2013 to about 118,000 in 2024 while the rental market kept running. Fair rules and a working market can coexist.

Sources: New York City Comptroller, 2025, NLIHC Advocates' Guide 2026

title: Claude Drop: housing-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
22.7 million U.S. renter households, 49% of renters, were cost-burdened in 2024, a record

Half the renters in America spend more than 30% of their income on housing. That's a record. When half the country is squeezed by the same bill, it isn't bad budgeting. It's a broken market. Fix it together.

Source: Harvard Joint Center for Housing Studies, State of the Nation's Housing 2026

title: Claude Drop: housing-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
12.1 million renter households, 26% of renters, paid more than half their income for housing in 2024

One renter household in four hands over half its paycheck to rent. The other half has to cover food, gas, medicine and kids. No amount of coupon clipping fixes that.

Source: Harvard Joint Center for Housing Studies, State of the Nation's Housing 2026

title: Claude Drop: housing-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
20.7 million homeowner households were cost-burdened in 2024, up 4 million since 2019

Owning isn't a shield anymore. Taxes, insurance and repairs push millions of homeowners past the limit. Owners and renters are in the same squeeze. That makes us allies.

Source: Harvard Joint Center for Housing Studies, State of the Nation's Housing 2026

title: Claude Drop: housing-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
The 2026 national housing wage for a modest two-bedroom rental is $34.73 an hour

That's what a full-time worker needs so rent stays under 30% of income. The average renter earns $24.84. The gap isn't laziness. It's a wage floor that sank while rents rose.

Source: National Low Income Housing Coalition, Out of Reach 2026

title: Claude Drop: housing-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
17 of the 25 most common U.S. occupations had median wages below the 2026 one-bedroom housing wage of $29.19

Cashiers, cooks, home health aides, warehouse workers. The jobs that keep America running don't pay enough to rent a one-bedroom. If work doesn't pay the rent, the deal is broken.

Source: National Low Income Housing Coalition, Out of Reach 2026

title: Claude Drop: housing-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Louisiana's 2026 two-bedroom housing wage is $21.88 an hour, while the state's mean renter wage is about $18.27

Louisiana renters are about $3.61 an hour short of a modest two-bedroom. Over a year of full-time work that's over $7,500. That's our fight in dollars and cents.

Source: National Low Income Housing Coalition, Out of Reach 2026: Louisiana
